chapters.name: Chapter 1: Getting ready to be recruited

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Rules first: eligibility and recruiting basics
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find the eligibility account and recruiting rules that apply to you.
This lesson builds toward: Given the college levels you are aiming for, you will identify which eligibility account you need and where to check recruiting contact rules for your sport, using official sites and your counselor, not AI or old articles, for rules and dates.
College sports have different organizations: NCAA Divisions I, II and III, the NAIA, and junior colleges. Each has its own academic and eligibility rules.
If you plan to play NCAA Division I or II, you will need an account with the NCAA Eligibility Center, which checks your academics and amateur status. The Eligibility Center site describes a Profile Page for younger students and Division III, and certification accounts for Division I and II. The NAIA has its own eligibility center; check its official site.
When college coaches may contact you, and how, depends on your sport and division and changes often. Do not rely on AI or old articles for dates; check ncaa.org, ask your high school coach and counselor, and keep your grades and core courses on track.
Step by step:
- Decide which levels you are aiming for.
- Visit the NCAA Eligibility Center and read which account fits you.
- Check the NAIA's own eligibility site if relevant.
- Ask your counselor about core courses and grades.
- Check recruiting contact rules for your sport on ncaa.org.
Words to know:
- Eligibility: meeting the academic and other rules needed to play college sports.
- NCAA Eligibility Center: the NCAA office where future college athletes register so their academics and amateur status can be checked.
- Division: a level of college sports, like NCAA Division I, II or III.
Official sources:
- NCAA Eligibility Center
- NCAA: Name, Image and Likeness (rules for recruits and athletes)
Try it now: Visit the NCAA Eligibility Center site and write which account type fits you. Then write one question about recruiting rules for your sport to ask your high school coach or counselor.
You can now find the eligibility account and official rules that apply to you.

check.q: Which organization has its own eligibility center separate from the NCAA?
check.why: The NAIA has its own eligibility center; check its official site.

check.q: An AI tells you the date college coaches can first call you. What do you do?
options: Check ncaa.org and ask your coach or counselor
Wait for a coach to call
check.why: Contact rules change often; check official sources, not AI.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Building your target school list
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build a spreadsheet of 15 schools that fit you athletically, academically and personally.
This lesson builds toward: Using Google Sheets and an AI assistant, you will build a target list of 15 schools marked reach, target or likely, with every school, coach name and roster detail checked on official school pages.
The right school is one where you can play, study what you want, afford it and be happy if sport ends. Aim for a mix: reach schools (a stretch), target schools (a good match) and likely schools (where you'd clearly contribute).
Make a Google Sheet with columns: School, Division, Location, Major you want, Roster need at your position, Academic fit, Cost notes, Coach name and email, Status. Get coach names and roster details from each school's official athletics website.
An AI assistant can suggest schools to research: "I'm a 5'9" soccer midfielder with a 3.5 GPA who wants to study nursing in the Southeast. Suggest 20 colleges with soccer programs at different levels to research." Then check each one yourself; AI lists can be out of date or wrong.
Step by step:
- Create the sheet with the columns above.
- Ask AI for schools to research.
- Check each school's official athletics and academic pages.
- Mark each as reach, target or likely.
- Keep 15 that truly fit.
Words to know:
- Target list: the schools you plan to contact.
- Roster: the list of players on a team; shows who is graduating at your position.
Try it now: Create your target list sheet. Use AI for ideas, verify ten schools on their official sites, and mark each as reach, target or likely.
You can now build and verify a balanced target school list.

check.q: What is a "likely" school on your target list?
options: A school where you would clearly contribute
A school with no team in your sport
check.why: Likely schools are where you would clearly contribute.

check.q: AI lists a school you have never heard of. What do you do?
options: Check its official athletics and academic pages first
check.why: AI lists can be out of date or wrong, so verify each school.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Your recruiting profile and highlight video
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Make a one-page recruiting profile and plan a two-to-four-minute highlight video.
This lesson builds toward: Using your true stats, grades and clips, you will create a one-page recruiting profile and a two-to-four-minute highlight video, with every stat true, best clips in the first 30 seconds, yourself marked before each clip, no home address, and a coach review.
A recruiting profile is one page: name, grad year, position, height and weight (honest), high school and club team, key stats, academic info (GPA, test scores if you have them, intended major), awards, your coaches' contact info, your highlight link, and your contact email.
A highlight video should be short, often two to four minutes, with your best clips in the first 30 seconds. Identify yourself before each clip with an arrow or circle. Add a full-game clip link if coaches in your sport like to see one. Ask your coach what coaches in your sport expect.
AI can help you write the profile from your notes and order your clips list. Every stat must be true and verifiable; coaches check with your coaches. Keep private details like home address off the profile.
Step by step:
- Gather your true stats, grades and awards.
- Ask AI to format a one-page profile.
- Pick your best clips and put the top ones first.
- Mark yourself before each clip.
- Ask your coach to review both.
Words to know:
- Recruiting profile: a one-page summary of you as an athlete and student for college coaches.
- Highlight video: a short video of your best plays.
Try it now: Use AI to turn your notes into a one-page profile. Write your clip list with the best five first, and ask your coach to review both.
You can now create an honest recruiting profile and a strong highlight video plan.

check.q: Why mark yourself before each clip?
options: So coaches know which player you are
check.why: An arrow or circle helps coaches find you right away.

check.q: Your listed 40-yard time is faster than you have ever run. What do you do?
options: Keep it; coaches will not check
Change it to your true, verifiable time
Round it down a bit more
check.why: Every stat must be true; coaches check with your coaches.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Contacting coaches and staying organized

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Writing personal emails to coaches with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a short, personal introduction email to a college coach.
This lesson builds toward: Using your profile and an AI draft, you will write personal introduction emails to three college coaches, under 150 words each, with a clear subject line and one true, specific reason for each school, sent by you from a professional email.
Coaches get many emails. Short and personal wins. Include: subject line with grad year, position and key info ("2027 Midfielder | 3.5 GPA | Metro FC Club Team"); why you're interested in their school specifically; your key stats and academics; your highlight link and profile; your upcoming schedule (tournaments, showcases); and your coach's contact.
Ask an AI assistant: "Write a short email to the head soccer coach at [school]. Use my profile below. Mention that I'm interested in their nursing program and their possession style. Under 150 words." Then make it yours and check every detail.
Send from a professional email you check daily. Never send the exact same email to every school; coaches can tell. Send it yourself, not your parents, and follow up politely after a couple of weeks with new information, like a new highlight.
Step by step:
- Write a clear subject line.
- Ask AI for a draft under 150 words using your profile.
- Add one true, specific reason for that school.
- Check every detail and the coach's name.
- Send from your professional email; follow up with new info.
Words to know:
- Subject line: the short title of an email; the first thing a coach sees.
- Showcase: an event where athletes play in front of college coaches.
Try it now: Write emails to three coaches on your list with AI help. Make each one personal and have your coach or parent read one before sending.
You can now write a short, personal email to a college coach.

check.q: What should a coach email subject line include?
options: Grad year, position and key information
check.why: A clear subject line with grad year, position and key info gets noticed.

check.q: Two weeks after your email, there is no reply. What do you do?
options: Have your parent call the coach
Follow up politely with new information, like a new highlight
check.why: Follow up politely after a couple of weeks with something new.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Tracking your recruiting like a project
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Track every contact and next step in your recruiting sheet.
This lesson builds toward: Using your target list, you will track every contact, reply and next step with dates, updated weekly, with any paid recruiting service checked with your coach or counselor first.
Add tracking columns to your target list: Date contacted, Reply (yes/no), What they said, Next step, Next step date. Update it every week.
Watch for signs of real interest: personal replies, questions about your grades, invitations to camps or visits, or a coach watching you play. A generic camp ad is not the same as personal interest.
Recruiting can be stressful. Keep school and training first. Be careful with "recruiting services" that guarantee scholarships for a fee; check with your high school coach and counselor before paying anyone.
Step by step:
- Add tracking columns to your sheet.
- Log every email, reply and call.
- Write the next step and its date.
- Update weekly.
- Check any paid recruiting service with your coach first.
Words to know:
- Follow-up: a polite next message with new information.
- Recruiting service: a company that charges to help market you to colleges.
Try it now: Add the tracking columns to your sheet and log your three emails with a next step and date for each.
You can now track recruiting contacts and next steps like a project.

check.q: Which tracking column helps you remember what to do?
options: Next step and next step date
check.why: Next step and its date keep your recruiting moving.

check.q: You receive a generic camp ad from a college. What does it mean?
options: It is not the same as personal interest
The coach has seen your video
check.why: Personal replies and questions show real interest; a generic ad does not.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: For coaches: fair, organized scouting notes
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Organize scouting notes on prospects in a fair, consistent way.
This lesson builds toward: As a coach scouting prospects, you will organize scouting notes with the same criteria and a defined 1-to-5 scale for every player, with ratings from what you saw, AI used only to summarize notes, private data protected and bias checked.
Coaches who scout and recommend players can use the same tools. Create a sheet with the same criteria for every player: position skills, athleticism, game sense, coachability, academics and character notes from verified sources.
Use a simple 1-to-5 scale with written descriptions for each number, so ratings mean the same thing across evaluators. AI can summarize your written notes into a short report, but make sure ratings come from what you saw, not AI guesses.
Protect prospects' privacy: many are minors. Keep notes in approved, private places, don't paste personal details into AI tools, follow your organization's recruiting rules, and watch for bias, like judging by size alone or by highlight video quality instead of ability.
Step by step:
- Use the same criteria for every prospect.
- Define each number on a 1-5 scale.
- Write notes from what you saw.
- Use AI to summarize notes, not to rate.
- Keep data private; check for bias.
Words to know:
- Rubric: a scoring guide that describes what each score means.
- Coachability: how well a player listens to and uses feedback.
Try it now: Final task: athletes, finish your 15-school sheet, profile, highlight plan and three coach emails, plus a note on your eligibility account and where you checked rules. Coaches: build a 1-5 rubric with descriptions for five criteria.
You can now organize recruiting or scouting work clearly, honestly and fairly.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Eligibility and rules note No eligibility account named, or rules taken from AI or old articles. Names the eligibility account needed and the official source where recruiting rules were checked. Includes core course and grade checks done with the counselor. Target list Fewer than 15 schools, no reach, target and likely mix, or unchecked details. 15 schools with all columns, marked reach, target or likely, checked on official pages. Notes roster needs at the athlete's position and cost for each school. Profile and highlight video Untrue stats, private details, or best clips buried late in the video. A one-page honest profile and a 2-to-4-minute video with best clips first and the athlete marked, reviewed by a coach. Adds a full-game link if coaches in the sport expect one and keeps the profile up to date. Coach emails Generic, long, or sent by a parent. Three personal emails under 150 words with clear subject lines and a true reason for each school, sent by the athlete. Each includes the upcoming schedule and coach contact, and follow-up dates are logged. Tracking No tracking columns or next steps. Every contact logged with reply, next step and date. Updated weekly for a month, with real interest signs noted. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Why write a description for each number on the 1-to-5 scale?
options: So ratings mean the same thing across evaluators
check.why: Defined numbers keep ratings consistent between coaches.

check.q: A prospect is short but plays smart and wins every battle. How do you rate game sense?
options: Based on what you saw, not size
check.why: Judging by size alone is a form of bias.
